index.answer: No, it leaks in the first block: the residual connection and the query of position i both carry piece i into the output at position i. Each block computes its input plus what attention gathers, so the vector at position i after the first block still holds piece i, whatever the attention weights are. theory.title: Five Predictions in Two Inputs
overview: A batch holds two inputs. In input A, four positions were chosen for prediction, and the model gives their original pieces probabilities 0.5, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. In input B, one position was chosen, and the model gives its original piece probability 0.125. No other position has a loss.

setup.p: Two training scripts turn these into one batch loss.

list: **Script 1** averages the losses of all five predictions.
**Script 2** averages the losses within each input, then averages the two inputs.

prompt.p: What loss does script 1 report? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: Each loss is $-\ln p$. The five probabilities are powers of $\tfrac12$, so the losses are multiples of $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$:
Script 1 divides their total by 5:

prompt.p: What loss does script 2 report?

answer.p: Input A averages to $6 \ln 2 / 4 = 1.5 \ln 2$, and input B is its one loss, $3 \ln 2$. The mean of the two is
The model and its predictions are the same, yet script 2 reports a loss 25% higher, because it counts B's poor prediction more heavily.

prompt.p: Under script 2, how many times as much does B's prediction count as one of A's? Say which script gives every prediction the same weight, and what goes wrong with the other one when the number of chosen positions varies a lot from input to input.

answer.p: Script 2 gives each input half of the loss, and splits that half among the input's predictions. Each of A's four predictions gets $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac18$ and B's single one gets $\tfrac12$, four times as much. Script 1 gives all five $\tfrac15$.

The weights show up in training. Raising B's probability from 0.125 to 0.5 lowers B's loss by $2 \ln 2$, and script 1 falls by $2 \ln 2 / 5 \approx 0.277$ while script 2 falls by $2 \ln 2 / 2 \approx 0.693$. Raising one of A's 0.25 to 0.5 lowers that loss by $\ln 2$, and the two scripts fall by $0.139$ and $0.087$. So script 2 pays 8 times as much for the first fix as for the second, where script 1 pays only the factor of 2 that the two losses differ by.

Script 1 is the average that `cross_entropy` with `ignore_index=-100` computes over the flattened batch, and BERT's own pretraining code also divides the summed loss by the number of predictions in the batch. When the number of chosen positions varies, an input with two predictions gets the same half of script 2's loss as an input with twenty. Each of its two predictions then pulls as hard as ten of the other input's, and the loss script 2 reports moves with how the positions happened to be chosen.

theory.title: A nan Every Few Dozen Steps
overview: A team pretrains a small BERT on product titles from an online shop. After tokenization every title is 6 pieces, so each input is `[CLS]`, 6 pieces and `[SEP]`, and a batch holds 4 titles. The collator works like Hugging Face's: it flips a 15% coin at each of the 24 title pieces in the batch, never at `[CLS]` or `[SEP]`, and gives every unchosen position the label $-100$. The loss is

setup.p: with the default `ignore_index=-100`. Every so often the logged loss is `nan`. The training loop skips any step whose loss is not finite, and the weights never blow up.

prompt.p: Where does the `nan` come from?

answer.p: `cross_entropy` with `ignore_index=-100` adds up the losses at the labeled positions and divides by how many there are. When none of the 24 coins comes up, every label in the batch is $-100$, so the sum has no terms and the count is 0. The mean is $0/0$, which is `nan`. Nothing is wrong with the model or the learning rate: those steps have no prediction to learn from.

prompt.p: What is the probability that a given step logs `nan`? About how many of 5,000 steps will?

answer.p: The 24 coins are independent and each comes up tails with probability 0.85, so
about one step in 49, or roughly 100 of 5,000 steps.

prompt.p: On a given step, what is the probability that one particular title gets no target at all? What does that mean for the steps that do run?

answer.p: A title has 6 coins, so it gets no target with probability

On average $4 \times 0.377 \approx 1.5$ of the 4 titles in every batch contribute no prediction. The model still runs on them, but nothing in such a title reaches the loss, since the inputs of a batch never attend to each other. So more than a third of the work on title pieces trains nothing, and the `nan` steps are only the case where all four titles miss at once. The coin gives 15% of the pieces on average, $24 \times 0.15 = 3.6$ targets per batch, but on inputs this short the count is often 0 per title.

prompt.p: BERT's original code instead chooses a fixed number of positions per input, $k = \max(1, \operatorname{round}(0.15\,n))$, where $n$ is the length of the input. What does that give for these titles, and why can it never produce the `nan`? A teammate suggests raising the coin to 32% instead. What would that do?

answer.p: Each input has 6 choosable pieces (never `[CLS]` or `[SEP]`), and $0.15 \cdot 6 = 0.9$ rounds to 1, so every title gets one target and every batch gets 4. The share hidden is $1/6 \approx 17\%$, close to the 15% aimed for, and no title or batch is ever left without a target, so the count in the mean is always 4 and never 0.

A 32% coin makes the `nan` rare, $0.68^{24} \approx 10^{-4}$, about one step in 10,000. But it hides about a third of every title on average, more than twice as much context as the recipe intends, and a title still gets no target with probability $0.68^6 \approx 0.10$. The fixed count fixes the cause, which is that the number of targets per input can be 0, without changing how much of each input is hidden.

and in the same way $bb$ gets $0.64$ while $ab$ and $ba$ get $0.2 \cdot 0.2 = 0.04$. The total is
So $e^{\text{PLL}}$ is not a probability: it adds up to more than 1, and it gives $aa$ 0.64 where the true probability is 0.4.

**(b)** For the family $P(aa) = P(bb) = \tfrac{1 + c}{4}$ and $P(ab) = P(ba) = \tfrac{1 - c}{4}$, with $0 \le c \le 1$, the four values of $e^{\text{PLL}}$ add up to $1 + c^2$.

and by independence the last product is $P(uv)$.

**(b)** Each piece is $a$ with probability $\tfrac{1+c}{4} + \tfrac{1-c}{4} = \tfrac12$. A matching piece then has conditional probability $\tfrac{1+c}{4} / \tfrac12 = \tfrac{1+c}{2}$, and a different piece $\tfrac{1-c}{2}$. Adding the four sentences,

At $c = 0$ the pieces are independent and the total is 1, as in (a). The table above is $c = 0.6$, giving $1.36$. At $c = 1$ only $aa$ and $bb$ occur, each piece is certain given the other, and both sentences get $e^{\text{PLL}} = 1$ though each has probability $\tfrac12$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

prompt.p: Explain how PLL scores a sentence that contains a rare word the tokenizer splits into several pieces, such as `rey`, `##k`, `##ja`, `##vik`, and compare it with the chain rule a left-to-right model uses.

answer.p: PLL hides one piece at a time, and the other pieces of the same word stay visible. With `##k`, `##ja` and `##vik` in view, `rey` is nearly certain, and the same holds for each of the others, so each of the four terms is close to $\ln 1 = 0$. The word costs almost nothing in the PLL however rare it is, which is the $c = 1$ case of (b): pieces that determine each other.

A left-to-right model scores the same word by the chain rule: the log probability of `rey` given the words to its left, plus that of `##k` given those words and `rey`, and so on. Its first term is paid before any of the word is seen, and for a rare word that term is large and negative. Its later terms are near 0 as in PLL, but the first one charges for the word's rarity once. PLL never charges it, so it rates sentences with long, rare multi-piece words too highly. A fix that keeps BERT is to hide all the pieces of a word that lie to the right of the piece being scored, so that each word pays for its first piece the way the chain rule does.

answer.p: **80/0/20.** A target that shows a piece always shows its original, so $P(O = s \mid S = s) = 1$ for every $q_s$. The best output at any visible position is the piece it shows, with certainty. Copying solves every kept target, so those targets teach nothing about language, and the model never needs the context to judge a visible piece.

**80/20/0.** A target that shows a piece shows a random one, so $P(O = s, S = s) = q_s / V$ and $P(S = s) = 1 / V$, which gives $P(O = s \mid S = s) = q_s$. The shown piece carries no information, and the model learns to predict every visible position from the context alone, as if the piece were not there. After pretraining every input piece is real, so this teaches the model to distrust the one piece of evidence it will always have.

**80/10/10.** The formula from the first part sits between the two. A visible piece that the context finds plausible is almost surely real and is nearly copied. One the context finds very unlikely is mostly ignored. To make that call the model has to judge every visible piece against its context, which is the skill the 10% kept and the 10% random pieces teach together. Neither half does it alone.
